summary: Burning Activity Calendar is a web application that turns NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots into a month-by-year calendar of burning activity for any area a user draws on a map. The satellite fire record is split between MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012), which detect fires very differently, so raw counts jump when the sensor changes. We collapse both to a common unit (fire cell-days on a 0.1 degree grid), learn how MODIS relates to VIIRS during the years both satellites fly, correct that relationship region by region, and convert 2000-2011 MODIS into VIIRS-equivalent values. The result is one consistent 26-year series covering South, Central and North America. For any area, the app shows when the fire season peaks, which months were unusual compared with the historical median, the most active months and years, and lets users download the data. Tested on years the model never saw (2019-2026), the harmonized series has a 7.7% monthly error, versus 59.8% using raw MODIS. This gives emergency responders, scientists and land managers a consistent long-term picture of when and where burning happens.
details:
Live demo with NOAA-20 extension (after S-NPP), no installation needed: https://burning-activity-calendar-noaa20.onrender.com (free hosting, so the first load can take about a minute). Source code: https://github.com/biombo-anexo/burning-activity-calendar

What it does

Burning Activity Calendar is a web app that shows when and where vegetation burns. A user draws a rectangle or polygon on a map (or picks a quick area such as Colombia, the Brazilian Amazon, the Cerrado, Mexico or Alaska) and gets a calendar of fire activity, months by years, from November 2000 to November 2026. The app explains in plain language when the fire season peaks, how the latest month compares with what is usual, and which years were the most and least active. An anomaly view colours each month against the historical median, a seasonal chart compares any year with the typical year, and rankings list the most active months and years. Users can download a monthly summary (CSV), the daily cell-level data (CSV) and an image of the calendar (PNG).

How it works

1. Data: NASA FIRMS archive and near-real-time hotspots from MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra and Aqua, 1 km) and VIIRS S-NPP (375 m) for South America and for North and Central America: 92 million detections.

2. Cleaning: only presumed vegetation fires are kept (FIRMS type 0); low-confidence detections and static sources such as gas flares and volcanoes are removed.

3. Common unit: a fire cell-day, meaning a 0.1 degree (about 11 km) cell with at least one detection on a given day. This makes sensors with different pixel sizes comparable.

4. Calibration: during 2012-2026, when both sensors fly, the app learns how many VIIRS cell-days correspond to the MODIS cell-days in each 1 degree block and month. Three models are compared (ratio, power law, seasonal power law) and the winner is chosen on held-out years.

5. Regional correction: the MODIS-to-VIIRS relation differs by region (VIIRS adds about 2.2 times more detections in tropical farmland but much less in boreal forests), so each 1 degree block gets a correction factor, shrunk towards its 5 degree region so that areas with little data stay stable.

6. Terra-only correction: before July 2002 only one MODIS satellite flew, so those months are scaled by the measured two-satellite ratio for that calendar month.

7. Quality flags: every month is marked as normal, Terra-only, near-real-time (provisional), partial, or affected by a suspected satellite outage, and the calendar shows these flags.

Validation

The model was trained on 2012-2018 and tested on 2019-2026, years it never saw. The monthly error over the whole area is 7.7%, compared with 59.8% if raw MODIS were used. The yearly error for a 1 degree area falls from 27.6% to 16.2% with the regional correction. As an independent check, raw MODIS (one sensor over both periods) and the harmonized series show the same change in fire activity between 2003-2011 and 2013-2025 within 3% in 13 of the 16 regions tested. Running the Colombia border on this continental dataset and on an earlier Colombia-only download gives totals 0.1% apart. 52 automated tests cover the method and the app.

Benefits and impact

Fire managers, early-warning teams, scientists and land managers get one consistent 26-year record instead of two incompatible ones, so they can see the normal fire season of any area, spot unusual months and plan monitoring for critical periods. The results are transparent: the app shows which years are estimates from MODIS and how accurate the method is.

Tools

Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, DuckDB, PyArrow), FastAPI and Uvicorn for the server, Leaflet and Leaflet.draw for the map, HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the interface, and pytest for testing.

Limitations

Values before 2012 are estimates converted from MODIS. The record ends on 2 November 2026 because VIIRS S-NPP stopped delivering data; continuing it requires calibrating NOAA-20 or NOAA-21. Some regional bias remains (Western United States +16%, Bolivian lowlands and Canadian boreal forest -7% in the independent check). Cell-days measure detected fire activity, not burned area.

Accessibility (colour-blind safety): fire activity uses the Viridis ramp and anomalies use the ColorBrewer purple-orange (PuOr) ramp, both designed for colour-vision deficiency with a steady lightness ramp, so they also read in greyscale. We checked them by simulating protanopia, deuteranopia and tritanopia (Machado et al. 2009): neighbouring colours stay at least 8.7 (Viridis) and 10.3 (PuOr) Delta-E units apart. No information depends on colour alone: data gaps use a solid outline, Terra-only months a dashed border, provisional months italics, and every cell shows its value.

Next step: NOAA-20 carries the same VIIRS instrument and overlaps S-NPP from April 2018, so the record can be continued past 2 November 2026 by calibrating NOAA-20 against S-NPP on that overlap with the same held-out validation. We downloaded the NOAA-20 archive but did not finish this before the deadline.
